stories.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
stories.summary: The post Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A woman wearing a suit jacket sits beside a woman wearing a brown shirt, behind a curved wooden table with laptops, microphones, and nameplates as King speaks during a board meeting, filmed by cameras in the foreground.
stories.body:
For much of the past year, members have worked with the Election Integrity Network on shared priorities, including a controversial, error-prone software tool used to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.

In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.

The board sets the swing state’s election rules , oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.

Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.

The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes.

At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA , Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.

At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.

The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.

EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.

“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”

The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.

“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.”

Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday , in part to discuss personnel matters .

In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.

“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for amazing performances, not threats of termination.”

In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run.

Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and affiliated groups.

King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.

“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.”

When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.

Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to EIN.

Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed questions, put a post on X celebrating EIN’s work with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer anyone?”

Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”

EIN has been deeply entwined with conservatives’ efforts to reshape Georgia elections since at least 2024.

That year, ProPublica’s reporting revealed, EIN members secretly pushed a rule through the State Election Board allowing local officials to potentially delay certifying the state’s vote count. A court subsequently struck down the change, which experts had warned could enable county election boards to disrupt certifying the election if Trump had lost .

In late 2025, the board played a role in instigating the Trump administration’s unprecedented effort to reinvestigate alleged 2020 voting irregularities , formally asking the Justice Department to obtain Fulton County election records subsequently seized by the FBI. It was a move pushed by the EIN. The affidavit authorizing the raid cited Johnston and King as witnesses. The affidavit also cited a report put together by an EIN researcher compiling activists’ debunked allegations of fraud.

In recent months, EIN’s allies and participants at the state board pushed counties to use ELLY, a tool developed by an EIN member, to search voter rolls for signs of fraud and purge suspect registrants.

ELLY aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources, but doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers or full dates of birth. As a result, voting rights groups have said, ELLY often erroneously flags legitimate voters.

Nonetheless, before the midterms, the State Election Board’s investigative staff pressured Chatham County, a Democratic stronghold, to purge more than 200 registered voters that the tool identified as questionable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported .

After the election, a Forsyth County election board member who is also a member of EIN submitted ELLY data questioning the validity of over 60 ballots, including four cast by people who were supposedly dead. ProPublica found that all four were, in fact, alive. The board rejected the challenges.

EIN members and state board officials have defended ELLY’s accuracy .

The EIN’s connections to the board carry additional importance in light of last week’s election results, in which Democrats wrested control of all statewide offices and the state House from Republicans. The House appoints a member to the State Election Board , opening the door to change.

Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms ran on a platform that promised a new approach to the election board.

“The State Election Board has become mired in political games, conspiracy theories, and partisan interference,” the platform stated . Bottoms’ platform pledged that she would “work with the General Assembly to eliminate the current State Election Board and replace it with a stronger, more independent election oversight structure that is insulated from partisan manipulation.”

Fervier is part of the board’s four-member Republican majority, but he has clashed repeatedly with Johnston, King and Mills and has effectively been relegated to a member of the minority at times.

Emails and communications between board members and staff obtained by ProPublica via public records requests show that Fervier and other board members who oppose steps supported by the EIN have been excluded from some board hiring decisions.

Earlier this year, Fervier publicly accused Mills of going beyond what the board had authorized in calling for the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to intervene to assess the security of the state’s voting machines.

“Activists should not control the board,” he told ProPublica. “I’m really looking forward to this meeting because I think that we’re going to address some issues that should have been addressed awhile ago.”

stories.body:
Diabetes is the leading cause of death in South Africa. But many people with the condition don’t know they have it. The International Federation of Diabetes has estimated that 60% to 70% of people with diabetes remain undiagnosed .

One reason is that the disease often develops without significant symptoms. There are two main types of diabetes which develop in different ways. Type 2 diabetes is the most common and develops when the cells become less responsive to insulin.

Insulin is a hormone that is produced by the pancreas. It plays a vital role in controlling the amount of sugar (glucose) in our blood. The food we eat is broken down into glucose, which enters the bloodstream and provides the body with energy.

However, glucose needs help to move from the blood into the body’s cells where it can be used for fuel. Insulin acts as a key which unlocks the cells and allows the glucose to enter and provide the fuel needed for organs and tissues to function. When there is more glucose than needed, the insulin can direct the excess to the liver for storage and later use.

Diabetes develops when this system does not work properly.

Read more: 79 deaths a day: South Africa’s diabetes crisis needs a new strategy

One of the biggest dangers of diabetes is that people can live with high glucose levels for many years without any symptoms . During this time the excess glucose can damage blood vessels throughout the body. This, in turn, can lead to blurred vision and nerve, heart and kidney damage.

This is why it is important to detect diabetes early. Treatment and lifestyle changes can be introduced to reduce the risk of life-threatening complications.

But many communities don’t have easy access to routine screening or healthcare. Even when routine screening is available, it is often inconsistent and only performed on individuals who already have complications. Point-of-care, finger-prick tests are not uniformly available at health facilities and the quality of testing is not maintained.

Our research at the SAMRC/CPUT Cardiometabolic Health Research Unit aims to study ways of identifying people living with diabetes before they develop complications. Over the years, we have developed expertise in identifying early biological indicators of diabetes. We’ve recognised pitfalls in current tests which are not always appropriate for all populations.

To address this gap we recently investigated simple screening tools which could be used in community clinics that do not have access to laboratories. Our study found that simple measurements, such as waist circumference, could be used to identify those at risk of developing diabetes.

This is important because South Africa must move beyond a symptom driven approach to diabetes detection, and towards risk-based screening.

The challenges with testing

There are four tests used to diagnose diabetes in South Africa. These are the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), fasting glucose, random glucose and glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c). Each of these has advantages and challenges.

The OGTT can identify patients at an early stage of the disease. But it is time consuming and requires patients to fast overnight. Before the test, glucose levels must be tested and then patients ingest 75g of glucose. Patients wait two hours for the second glucose sample to be taken. By comparing the two glucose levels doctors can see how the body handled the concentrated glucose intake. This is the gold standard test. But practically it is difficult to implement in primary healthcare settings.

The random blood glucose test does not need fasting, it only requires a blood sample. But it is influenced by food intake, which is difficult to control and can lead to unreliable results. The fasting blood glucose requires an overnight fast and tests must often be repeated as results can be variable. There are many point-of-care glucose tests which people can use at home to monitor glucose levels but these too can give false results if done incorrectly .

Tests for glycated haemoglobin (known as HbA1c) measure the average blood sugar levels over the past two to three months by determining how much excess sugar is stuck to the haemoglobin in the red blood cell. It does not require fasting and could be used to identify people with pre-diabetes as it measures how the body has handled glucose intake over time. Internationally, it has been recommended that a person has diabetes if more than 6.5% of their haemoglobin has blood sugar attached. However, our earlier research has shown that this level may miss early diabetic risk in mixed ancestry communities and that a level of 6.1% would be more appropriate. This has been supported by more recent research which proposed that 6.1% is far more appropriate for early detection and to screen those who remain undiagnosed .

There’s another snag with this test. HbA1c can be tested using point-of-care instruments. But these are not consistently used in South Africa. The test is expensive, and usually performed in laboratories. It is not widely available in public clinics. HbA1c results can also be affected by many conditions such as iron deficiency anaemia, chronic kidney disease or when the lifespan of a red cell is lower than normal.

This means that the test is not equally reliable across different population groups, particularly in Africa. In response to these limitations, the National Department of Health suggested in 2017 that the HbA1c should not be used as the primary diagnostic test unless evidence-based population studies have been conducted.

Our unit’s previous research supports this and recommends that HbA1c in combination with other tests such as glycated albumin may improve the early detection of diabetes.

One of our goals is to identify simple measurements which can be used in community clinics to identify risk of diabetes before the development of complications.

Recent research conducted in our laboratory has identified waist circumference, waist to height ratio and excess abdominal fat to be closely associated with insulin resistance and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. This simple measurement could be included in routine community health screening. It would allow those with increased waist circumference together with other risk factors such as high blood pressure and family history to be referred for further glucose testing.

Waist circumference cannot diagnose diabetes, but can be valuable in identifying those at risk, and with simple lifestyle changes and exercise this could be reversed.

Read more: Fruit juices in South Africa are getting a free ride: why they should have the same health warning labels as fizzy drinks

What needs to be done

South Africa’s diabetes crisis requires a multi-pronged approach.

Simple, inexpensive tests and screening tools are required to detect undiagnosed people living with diabetes in South Africa. Research must identify these tests, and provide evidence that they work and can be used effectively.

The country needs strong public health campaigns, simple and accessible screening programmes and improved access to diagnostic testing and treatment.

This requires commitment from policymakers, citizens, healthcare workers and researchers.

stories.title: Defying Voters, Washington and Jerusalem Are Moving Closer
stories.summary: The Trump administration is pushing for more, not less, military cooperation with Israel. The post Defying Voters, Washington and Jerusalem Are Moving Closer appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump (Shutterstock)

Two elections in eight days sent leaders the same message, and neither country got a clean answer.

On November 3, American voters delivered a landslide. Democrats flipped eight Senate seats and now hold a 55-44 majority. They have won the House as well, with fewer than 20 races still uncalled, and they are on track to match or pass the 257 seats Democrats won in 2008. They won Senate seats in states Trump carried by double digits in 2024, including Texas, for the first time since 1988 . The president is trying to distance himself from the result.

A week earlier, Israelis voted on October 27 and could not decide. Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud won 27 seats, the most of any party , but his right-wing and ultra-Orthodox bloc holds only 53 of 120, eight short of a majority and down from 64 in 2022. Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist bloc holds 48, and Arab parties hold a record 19. On November 8, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot the first chance to form a government after 67 lawmakers endorsed him , against 46 for Netanyahu, who stays on as caretaker prime minister in the meanwhile.

Israel’s system explains why. Voters choose a party list, and seats are divided proportionally nationwide, so no party has ever won a majority alone. Israel’s president asks the candidate with the best chance of assembling 61 seats to form a government, which usually means the leader of the largest party, though not this time. That candidate gets 28 days, extendable by 14. If the candidate fails, another gets a turn, and if that fails too, the country goes to a new election. The 67 endorsements include Arab-led parties, but Eisenkot has ruled out governing with them , so they are not likely to be part of his majority. His clearest path to 61 runs through the two ultra-Orthodox parties that sit in Netanyahu’s bloc. Otherwise he would need a minority government that survives a no-confidence vote. If he fails, Netanyahu is next in line. Each side needs people it has sworn it will not work with.

Voters in both countries have just withheld a mandate. Washington and Jerusalem are, meanwhile, binding their militaries together in a way that is harder to undo than any election. The first signal came on Monday in Paris, where Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that Israel is rich enough to buy American weapons and that President Trump wants U.S. military financing to end “as soon as possible.” That financing is about $3.8 billion a year under a 10-year agreement that expires in September 2028: $3.3 billion for weapons purchases and $500 million for missile defense.

Rubio said the terms are being worked out in a new memorandum of understanding, that Israel could “absolutely” stop receiving aid by the end of the year if it chose, and that the deal could include joint weapons production. “We’ll negotiate the timeline,” he said. Trump had said the week before that the two countries had agreed to end the aid by the end of 2026, which according to The Times of Israel surprised officials on both sides. Netanyahu has proposed phasing it out over about a decade.

That sounds like distance. Read together with the defense bill, it looks more like a change of form: military grants give way to joint production and shared technology. Critics of the aid may welcome the end of grants. The question is what replaces them, and who gets a say. The vehicle is the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The House passed the FY2027 bill, 216 to 212 , with $750 million for joint programs with Israel, including $500 million for missile defense, the figure the current agreement already commits, plus counter-drone, tunnel, and emerging-technology work. The Senate Armed Services Committee’s version carries its own provisions for the military support of Israel.

Both include the Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative , which would make the Pentagon designate an executive agent to coordinate joint research, testing, integration, and industrial cooperation—which would move coordination out of the realm of foreign aid and into the more opaque world of Pentagon contracts. The House bill also expands intelligence sharing with Israel and creates an Abraham Accords defense initiative. And U.S. taxpayers pay the bill.

The Senate has not passed its version. A July vote to begin debate failed 50 to 46 , and the final text is expected to be a compromise drafted by the Armed Services Committee leaders in the lame-duck session , competing for floor time with a December 11 government funding deadline. What that text will contain on Israel is not yet clear.

Supporters, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), say that the provisions make existing cooperation more efficient and were co-sponsored by members of both parties. They also argue that the United States gets a multiple return in technology and lessons from combat. Critics disagree. Representatives across the aisle, Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Ro Khanna (D-CA), tried to strike the section and failed . Massie warned that writing it into law would make it harder for a future administration to reverse it.

The lobby from AIPAC that praised these provisions had a poor election. According to an analysis from Responsible Statecraft , its super PAC and affiliated groups spent about $84 million this cycle, and nearly two-thirds of it, about $55 million, went to candidates who lost. The largest effort, more than $31 million, failed to stop Abdul El-Sayed from winning Michigan’s Senate seat in both the primary and the general election. “Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice ,” he told AIPAC in his victory speech. James Talarico won Texas after saying he had never taken AIPAC’s money and would not take it in his campaign. A Democratic strategist told Agence France-Presse that campaigns that once coveted AIPAC’s support now see it as a liability. Opinion is moving too: in the Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey, Americans’ favorability toward Israel averaged 44 out of 100 this year, a record low , down from 58 in 2022, and among Democrats it fell from 52 to 30.

Voters in both countries have just reopened the question of who governs and on what terms. A provision written into a defense bill by a Congress whose majority is about to change closes it for them. The final bill is expected to come together before the new Congress is sworn in.

The rebuke, though, is not symbolic. The new Democratic majority takes office in January, and the final NDAA text is not yet settled. Constituents who want their representatives to explain what the Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative does, and whether it should carry a review date, still have a few weeks to ask.

stories.title: Power Shift: State Election Wins Open Path for Climate Progress
stories.summary: In the U.S. midterm elections, Democrats won control of governorships and state legislatures across the country. At a time of public outcry over data centers and rising electricity costs, incoming leaders will have a mandate to rein in polluters, constrain utilities, and advance clean energy. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Keisha Lance Bottoms, governor-elect of Georgia, celebrating her victory in Atlanta on election night. Paras Griffin / Getty Images

OPINION

In the U.S. midterm elections, Democrats won control of governorships and state legislatures across the country. At a time of public outcry over data centers and rising electricity costs, incoming leaders will have a mandate to rein in polluters, constrain utilities, and advance clean energy.

By Michael Gerrard • November 12, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

After their sweeping victories in the midterm elections, Democrats will control both houses of Congress, meaning they will be able to shape the budget, conduct vigorous oversight and investigations, and refuse to confirm nominees for judgeships and other high positions — but their power will be limited. Any ambitious new bill to tackle climate change, for example, will face President Trump’s veto pen.

But there are other ways for Democrats to make progress on climate, energy, and the environment — by wielding their newfound power in the states. In the November 3 elections, Democrats flipped control of governors’ offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and Texas, and are on track to win in Alaska, where votes are still being counted. They also attained trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both houses of the state legislature — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin.

This brings to 29 or 30 the number of states that will have Democratic governors in January, and to 22 the states in which Democrats have unified control of government. Meanwhile, Republican trifectas were broken in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

In Texas, which is facing a massive buildout of gas power, the incoming governor pledged a moratorium on new data centers.

While climate change was barely mentioned in these elections, many races were dominated by two closely related issues: data centers and utility regulation. Public outcry over the growth of data centers, which are driving ever more burning of natural gas, and the rising cost of electricity mean that Democrats have a mandate to advance energy reforms in the states they control.

By one estimate, tech companies are intent on spending more than $647 billion over the coming years to develop natural gas infrastructure in the U.S. to serve the voracious power demands of data centers. The planned expansions would grow the existing fleet of gas generators by roughly two-thirds. Natural gas is already the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. (behind petroleum, but far greater than coal), and this investment would lock in its use for decades.

Against this backdrop, public opposition to data centers has rocketed. In the midterm elections, ballot measures to restrict data centers passed in 44 cities across the country and failed in only one. In her successful campaign for governor of Texas, which is facing the largest natural gas buildout in the nation, Gina Hinojosa pledged an immediate moratorium on new data centers. Many other winning candidates also promised more controls on data center construction.

State-level results of the 2026 midterm elections. States “flipped” where Democrats attained a governorship or a trifecta, meaning control of the governorship and both houses of the state legislature. Votes in the Alaska and Kansas gubernatorial races are still being counted, but at press time, Democrats lead in the vote totals. (Nebraska is labeled as having a trifecta, but it has a unicameral legislature.) Yale Environment 360 / Made with Flourish

Looking ahead, governors have the opportunity to appoint regulators who will further rein in data centers and the power utilities profiting from rising energy prices. Retail electricity rates are set by state public utility commissions, and in 38 states the commissioners are named by the governors. The newly elected Democratic governors of Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Maine all campaigned on promises to appoint commissioners who would work to favor the interests of ratepayers over those of monopoly utilities.

In practice, that could mean laying more costs on data centers and utility shareholders and less on consumers. It could also mean encouraging more rooftop and community solar to help lower electric bills. Utilities have long campaigned against such projects, which cut into their profits.

In Georgia, where commissioners are elected, Democrats just won a majority of seats on the five-member commission, promising greater scrutiny of the utilities. In Pennsylvania, legislation to lower power bills by reducing utility profits recently stalled in the Republican-controlled state senate, but under the new Democratic trifecta, this legislation is expected to be signed into law. In Michigan, about 80 percent of voters approved a ballot measure that will block utilities from campaign spending (which the utilities are already challenging in court). And in Colorado, voters rejected a ballot measure, championed by gas utilities, that would have established a “right to natural gas” and blocked local moves to phase out gas appliances.

Most federal environmental laws set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Beyond hemming in data centers and utilities, several other election outcomes hold promise for the environment. The Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry, has long consisted of three Republican members. A Democrat won election to the body with a platform that included capping orphan wells and banning gas flaring — two important means of stemming emissions from drilling. He can now put these issues on the agenda. His election also makes it possible for Democrats to win control of the commission in 2028.

Democratic candidates for state attorney general triumphed over Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas. Republican attorneys general have been at the forefront of litigation aimed at weakening environmental regulations, and they have moved in concert to protect oil and gas companies from being held accountable for climate damages. These states are expected to reverse their positions in many cases, which might tilt the scales in some.

What else might Democrats do with all their new power?

Given the focus of almost all campaigns on affordability, not many states are likely to adopt measures that would transparently increase consumer costs, such as a tax on carbon. However, states have many other tools. Most federal environmental statutes, such as the Clean Air Act, set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Demonstrators protest outside a forum for congressional candidates in Peekskill, New York, in October. Adam Gray / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Of the 10 states that burn the most coal for power, Democrats will now control the governor’s office in seven: Texas, Kentucky, Illinois, Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia, and Iowa. Governors in those states have considerable ability to shut coal plants down, for example, by setting air pollution standards that are too expensive for plants to meet.

If coal plants are to be shuttered and the use of natural gas slashed, the nation will need much more renewable energy, particularly wind and solar, to meet its growing electricity demand. One way to ramp up wind and solar is through renewable portfolio standards, which require utilities to acquire a certain percentage of their power from renewable sources. Today, 27 states have such standards, but many are so low that they have already been met. Democratic wins mean that more states can adopt renewable portfolio standards or strengthen and enforce those already on the books.

State leaders can also clear roadblocks for new renewable energy development. Over the last 30 years, more than 850 cities and counties have adopted restrictions on wind and solar, often spurred on by residents’ objections to large renewable installations proposed in their communities. In response, several states have adopted laws that centralize authority over such facilities, allowing them to override local bans. New York’s law has been especially successful at boosting wind and solar installations. Other states that now have Democratic trifectas could adopt similar laws.

States can encourage the uptake of electric vehicles by building more charging stations and providing rebates to EV buyers.

States may also encourage household solar by making it easier for homeowners to obtain approvals for rooftop arrays; enabling net metering; legalizing balcony solar; easing the siting of battery storage systems; and facilitating virtual power plants, which allow energy companies to link together and control home batteries, solar panels, thermostats, and other assets to balance the grid.

While states cannot require citizens to buy electric vehicles, they may encourage their uptake by building more charging stations, requiring new parking lots and garages to install fast chargers, and providing rebates to EV buyers to offset the recent loss of federal subsidies.

States can reduce emissions from the residential sector by incentivizing the installation of heat pumps, strengthening energy efficiency standards for buildings, and — though federal courts are split on whether this is permissible — barring new natural gas hookups.

These measures are only a fraction of what states can do. The Model Climate Laws Initiative, a joint project of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law and Environmental Advocates NY, has posted more than 2,000 model and actual state and local laws, and it stands ready to draft many more. Thoughtful policies aimed at cutting power bills, curbing pollution, and advancing clean energy have been circulating for a long time. It is time to put those policies into action.

stories.title: The False Promise of Pakistan’s Military
stories.summary: Washington should rethink its relationship with the generals. The post The False Promise of Pakistan’s Military appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. Vice President JD Vance (C) walks with Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshall Asim Munir (L), and Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar after arriving for talks with Iranian officials on April 11, 2026 at Islamabad, Pakistan. (Jacquelyn Martin - Pool/Getty Images)

Ever since Pakistan emerged as a mediator between Iran and the United States, Pakistan’s military chief, General Asim Munir, has been praised in Washington for being a statesman and a reliable security partner. President Trump has repeatedly called him his “favorite field marshal .”

Washington has made this bet before, and lost.

For decades, successive U.S. administrations supported Pakistan’s military rulers to advance their geopolitical agendas, overlooking—and at times reinforcing—authoritarianism in exchange for stability and cooperation.

The Trump administration is repeating the same bargain. It has defined counterterrorism, critical minerals, and managing regional competition with China among core U.S. interests. And yet, each of these is threatened by the very institution the United States has relied on to preserve them. The Democratic-controlled Congress now has an opportunity to reverse course.

Previously, the United States justified its support of the Pakistani military because it was perceived as a strong institution with widespread domestic support. Its legitimacy has eroded considerably since the ouster of former Prime Minister Imran Khan through a no-confidence vote in 2022. Many analysts believe that the military, after falling out with Khan, withdrew its backing and paved the way for his removal. A significant segment of the public turned against an institution long deemed untouchable.

For the United States to continue its support of Pakistan’s military risks its long-term relationship with a population of 250 million people, two-thirds of whom are under 30 and increasingly restless under growing military authoritarianism.

The problem directly affects Washington’s security interests.

The Pakistani military’s record as a counterterrorism partner should give Washington pause. Following 9/11, the military received billions of dollars in U.S. taxpayer money to combat the Taliban and al-Qaeda. Twenty years later, the Afghan Taliban returned to power, in part due to the Pakistani military’s patronage and protection of various Afghan Taliban factions within Pakistan.

This is not simply a story of past failure. Even today, the Pakistani military dominates counterterrorism policy in Pakistan’s two most restive provinces: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) and Balochistan. The military’s predominant use of coercive measures— mass displacements , drone warfare , and military operations in KPK—has failed to stem militancy and has instead caused widespread civilian suffering .

Balochistan, one of Pakistan’s most resource-rich provinces, has been racked by unrest and violence for decades. As in KPK, security policy in Balochistan is under the strict control of the military, with heavy army and Frontier Corps deployments.

Rather than take seriously the legitimate grievances of the people—failed governance, abysmal human development indicators, resource exploitation without local input or benefit—the Pakistani military has resorted to enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings , and detentions of Baloch students and activists. Earlier this year, Mahrang Baloch, a Nobel Peace Prize nominee who has led a peaceful movement for Baloch rights, was sentenced to life in prison in a secret trial.

In both provinces, militant violence has soared over the past two years.

The pervasive instability in Balochistan, in particular, threatens another major American interest: critical minerals, an essential part of the Trump administration’s National Security Strategy. In early 2026, the U.S. Export-Import Bank approved financing of $1.25 billion to support the mining of critical minerals at Reko Diq, home to one of the world’s largest untapped gold and copper deposits, located in the Chagai district of Balochistan.

However, increasing militancy in the province has exposed this investment to considerable risk and has already delayed the start of the project. Rather than learn from the Chinese experience—where billions of dollars of investments in Balochistan have foundered because of insecurity—the U.S. risks repeating it.

There is another contradiction in Washington’s approach.

For years, the United States saw Pakistan firmly in China’s orbit. In his second term, President Trump attempted to shift that approach and rebuild ties with the Pakistani military in order to preserve some measure of influence.

However, the Pakistani military is not just a security partner, it is the principal architect of Pakistan’s China policy. It manages defense acquisitions, economic projects, and the overall strategic relationship between the two countries.

That relationship continues to deepen. Following the India-Pakistan conflict in May 2025 in which Pakistan made effective use of Chinese technology and weapons, Pakistan’s defense budget increased by 20 percent. China, Pakistan’s largest arms supplier, stands to benefit from that expansion.

By building relations with the Pakistani military, the United States is not preserving influence. Rather, it is strengthening the very institution responsible for deepening ties with China.

An institution with little civilian oversight and accountability has little incentive to recalibrate a security paradigm that has allowed it to maintain its central and privileged relationship with the United States.

The United States holds significant influence over how its support is used: approval of F-16 sustainment sales, training through the IMET program, access to international financial systems, and diplomatic cover. It should condition that support on measurable human rights benchmarks, starting with the release of political prisoners, an end to military trials of civilians, and accountability for enforced disappearances. Such standards are rooted in Pakistan’s own constitution and its international commitments.

Democratic control of the House and Senate gives Congress an opportunity to reverse the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan’s military. Over the past two years, more than 100 Democrats in Congress signed letters calling out the Pakistani government’s human rights violations. Now, as incoming chairs of powerful committees, they can hold hearings, attach conditions to appropriations and defense bills, and investigate the Trump family’s crypto deals with foreign governments, including Pakistan’s.

Washington cannot determine Pakistan’s political future, nor should it try. But it can refuse to let American taxpayer dollars, military cooperation, and diplomatic backing prop up an increasingly unaccountable military establishment. Washington can keep treating Field Marshal Asim Munir as a security partner, even though his rule has not delivered stability. Or, instead of enabling military authoritarianism, it can recognize that America’s long-term interests lie in strengthening the civilian rule that Pakistanis have repeatedly voted for.

stories.body:
We are witnessing one of the biggest generational conflicts in decades: a global revolution against a gerontocracy.

John Last is a freelance journalist and former foreign correspondent living outside Ottawa, Canada.

Across Europe, young people are being arrested in their thousands. In Milan, jackbooted soldiers from the Italian military — average age, 38 — haul protesters, some of whom are as young as 12 and 13, away from picket lines and into armored vehicles. Italy’s government — average age, 60 — has passed a new decree allowing detainments for up to 24 hours without charge. Vandals can now be arrested 48 hours after their crimes; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, 53, has called for their parents to face financial penalties too.

Italy’s weekend of protests at the end of October, in at least a dozen major cities, was the most destructive in recent memory. In Milan, hooded youths looted the city’s luxury stores, pilfering products, one reporter wrote , “that they cannot afford and may never be able to buy.” But as shocking as Italy’s protests have been, they pale in comparison to those in France. Mobs of people have paralyzed city centers across the country for weeks. The grand streets of Paris have been blanketed in acrid smoke. French President Emmanuel Macron has accused an alliance of “radical far-left groups [and] criminals” of trying “to bring down the Republic.” Fifty-three police officers were injured over the course of a single weekend.

After more than a month, it is almost hard to believe that protests of this magnitude began over the failures of a university application portal . But by now, the grievances have multiplied: the high cost of fuel, the crowding of schools, the inaccessibility of housing, the growing precarity of work. In turn, the protests have taken on an existential desperation. An unmistakable vibe of despair permeates the masked protesters. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything,” one protester in Paris told the BBC. “It’s been too long, it’s been too much.”

“They” are the elder-elite of Europe, the now-aged baby boomers who greedily gobbled up the assets of their societies: a third of Italy’s housing stock; a quarter of France’s public spending; 98% of the average Spanish worker’s salary, in the form of monthly rent. While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — they cash in. Rising prices, precarious work, broken schools: As a generation, the boomers have remained largely unaffected while the value of their real estate and investments boomed. As their wealth and number grew, they came to set the agendas of unions, politicians and the media, and they bent the state to suppress any who would rally against them. They pioneered a playbook to extract the last cents of value from Europe’s bloated and aging welfare states before departing a world they leave on the threshold of self-destruction.

But the underclass in their wake cannot be restrained forever. In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long; like the dwarves of Moria, they accidentally unleashed a primal foe. “It has been called the children’s war,” La Repubblica reports : an insurgency against calcifying Western gerontocracies waged by their own offspring.

“While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — the now-aged baby boomers cash in.”

In some ways, generational inequality is felt before it can be measured. It is usually assumed that people naturally accumulate wealth over their lifetime, and that a person in their ‘70s should own more in assets than a relatively new worker in their ‘30s. But it wasn’t always so. Today’s old-age security is the result of a general crisis of elder poverty that proliferated across the Western world in the 1920s and ‘30s when people still literally worked themselves to death, or else died penniless. To solve this problem, states embraced a system of “asymmetric socialization,” according to Pieter Vanhuysse, a leading expert in political demography at the University of Southern Denmark. In short, the state took care of the elderly while the family was still mostly expected to take care of the young.

Today, it is hard to imagine a crisis of elder poverty on a similar scale to that of the 1930s, not least because the elderly account for such a large percentage of the population. In France and Italy, thanks to longer lifespans and low rates of reproduction, the number of citizens over 65 has doubled since the arrival of the boomer generation, born between 1946 and 1964, to one in five and one in four residents, respectively. Nor is the phenomenon limited to Europe. In the United States, where fertility rates are higher, the median age has risen by 10 years since 1960. There are fewer than a billion seniors in the world today; by 2060, that number is expected to double and account for a fifth of global population.

As seniors have exploded in number, they have exercised an ever-greater influence on politics. In France, the United Kingdom, Germany, the U.S. and many other developed nations, those aged 65 and over are between 10% and 20% more likely to vote than those aged 18-25. This has contributed to a shocking representative gap — people under 30 account for half of the world’s population but just 2% of its legislators. “There’s a clear representational deficit,” said Daniel Stockemer, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa. “It creates a problem that youth’s concerns are not taken sufficiently into consideration, that youth are not sufficiently included in decision-making processes.”

In a study of intergenerational fairness in state spending, Vanhuysse found a disproportionate favoritism toward the old in nearly all the countries surveyed. Nearly a quarter of young Europeans and nearly half of young Americans are struggling financially; they will also disproportionately bear the weight of the ecological destruction and public debt accumulated by the boomers.

France, where youth first took to the streets, is among the worst offenders. There, public debt now exceeds the value of its economy. In Vanhuysse’s index, it ranks just behind Japan for the disproportionate political power it grants the elderly — nearly two in five civil servants are over 50 , a number that has rapidly increased since 2011. Vanhuysse estimates roughly $5 is spent on elderly citizens for every $1 spent on youth. That is clearly evident in the crumbling, overcrowded schools and inadequate universities that first spurred young people onto the streets. State pensions, meanwhile, eat up a quarter of the country’s public spending — including a whole third of the education ministry’s budget.

“Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic.”

All of this would not be so galling if it were not for the fact that the generation now draining state coffers already benefited from an unprecedented golden age of growth. Boomers entered the workforce at the peak of unionization and enjoyed stable employment, wages that beat inflation and guaranteed pensions upon retirement. They were buying starter homes when housing could be had for just two or three years’ income. Today it is nearly 10 .

Boomers used this unprecedented growth to acquire assets well beyond their needs, sitting on valuable housing stock — 28% of family homes in the U.S., for example — desperately desired by the next generation. Then they leveraged those assets to squeeze younger generations. In Australia, seniors’ investment in rental properties has increased 1,500% at the same time as rents have nearly doubled. Where boomers were able to buy property cheaply and grow their money in investments, young people today spend a vast percentage of their earnings on rent — which, more often than not, is passive income for elderly landlords.

The result is a generation that feels it has been actively held back from achieving the same or better lives than their parents had by that same generation’s relentless extraction of money. Today, Vanhuysse found, a working person in France can expect their lifetime wealth to be 17% lower than that of a baby boomer. “That’s the same difference as being, today in France, a parent of two or a parent of none,” Vanhuysse said, or “of being — hold on for this — a migrant in France or not a migrant in France.”

Far from demonstrating concern for their children, boomers have become the archetype of the hectoring elder, demanding young people live in grim austerity or else be accused of moral failing. Meanwhile, they have led the charge against any policies that would address this imbalance: cuts to pension funding, extensions of the retirement age, freezes on rent, ends to tax breaks on capital gains, the construction of new housing. They have insisted on their right to rent-seek, to economically stunt their own children’s generation. And worse, they have, where possible, actively enshrined this inequality in law.

In the last 10 years, we’ve witnessed the emergence of a two-tiered economy: one offering secure employment and benefits to senior workers and a select few entrants, and a precarious gig economy for anyone else. Nowhere is this clearer than in Italy, which deflated a staggering 42% youth unemployment rate by passing a law allowing for short-term contracts — but only for workers hired after 2014. Today, 40% of those under 29 struggle with precarious employment, compared to just 5% of those over 50. Read Noema in print.

“In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long.”

Italy’s example is particularly stark, but this phenomenon plays out, with slight variations, across the Western world. As a union steward for Canada’s public broadcaster, I witnessed it firsthand: entrenched, often incompetent or disengaged elderly employees guaranteed healthy pensions and generous leave, enabled by the labor of an army of precarious young temps who were denied benefits, moved around and kept on exploitative short-term contracts, always hoping for some vanishing chance at security. The union fought tooth and nail to protect its incumbents; new workers, meanwhile, were expected to “do the time” in employment conditions that their elders had never been asked to endure.

The advent of AI and the ongoing liberalization of the marketplace have only added fuel to this dumpster fire, eliminating entry-level positions, complicating hiring with meaningless and time-consuming tests, and generally increasing the demands of employers. Those under 40 have probably lost count of the major economic disruptions they have been expected to adapt to (I can still remember when we were all being told to learn to code ). Now, still working their way toward stable jobs, home ownership and families, they are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their jobs, it may well collapse the economy instead.

Amid all this chaos, young people have been largely left to fend for themselves. It’s no coincidence that the underfunding of schools prompted this outbreak of violence: Despite a staggering rise in the diagnosis of learning disabilities, classes are often crammed with more students per teacher than ever before. Ten percent of teaching hours go untaught in France because of chronic teacher absenteeism. Parents, too, have taken leave of their responsibilities. One of the possible defenses of Vanhuysse’s “asymmetric socialization” is that, while seniors benefit from wealth transfers via taxes, parents transfer wealth to their children in the form of time — the equivalent of up to seven months’ wages a year, Vanhuysse estimated . But can we really say that’s the case when Gen Z and Gen Alpha are partly defined by the countless hours they were left glued to a screen, largely unsupervised, the unfiltered internet doing untold damage to their psyches?

Elders and politicians love to blame social media for a worrying rise in youth extremism and violence. But that’s not the only cause of the dark, seething nihilism at the heart of the generations now coming of age. Stockemer calls it a “vicious cycle of political alienation”: politicians serve elderly interests, young people disengage from politics and the next government has even less motivation to address their concerns. It has reached the point that politicians openly talk about younger generations as though they are an enemy and treat them accordingly by suspending many of their rights. Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has pioneered new methods in the overpolicing of the young: banning raves, lowering the age of criminal culpability and increasing juvenile detention by 50%. A communique from the October 17 Movement, one of the organizing groups behind Italy’s protests, captures the new reality: “A government that responds to the dissatisfaction of a generation with soldiers, handcuffs and decrees does not want to listen.”

But if governments won’t listen, why won’t the boomers who elect them? How can the outpouring of despair on the streets of Europe’s capitals not be enough to move them to cede some of their wealth to the next in line?

If it feels like theirs is a generation for whom no amount of money is enough, it may be because many of them genuinely feel that way, and for good reason. A lot of them grew up believing a millionaire was a rarefied thing. But now, a million dollars is barely enough to guarantee that a 65-year-old will spend their final years in comfort. The so-called “peak boomers” turning 65 between now and 2030 can reasonably expect to live another 20 years, and medical advancements may continue to extend their lifetimes. If they stop earning and investing, they will become victims of the same economic forces they unleashed on younger generations. High housing costs are preventing many seniors from downsizing as expected, high inflation is eating into the value of benefits and the side hustles and part-time jobs that once saved seniors from penury are scarcer than ever.

Looming behind this fear is the privatized eldercare market, which has become the norm in Europe as it has long been in North America. In European countries, the average home care starts at more than $1,000 per month and only climbs from there. Residential care can cost seniors or their families tens of thousands every year. The savings that were supposed to fund the “great wealth transfer” — the mass inheritance of more than $100 trillion in assets accumulated by boomers over their lifetime — are instead being siphoned away by an oligarchy of health care companies. No wonder medically assisted suicide is becoming more popular.

The reality is that neoliberal capitalism of the kind long championed by Macron has proven to be not very good at taking care of anyone except those now at liberty to make a lot more capital. The renowned French economist Thomas Piketty pointed out that the unprecedented 20% cut in per-student funding that prompted France’s protests came at a time when, according to some measures, “France has never been richer.” At the same time as public debt has ballooned out of control, the country’s privately held wealth has doubled in proportion to the country’s GDP, “with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes.” “The problem to solve,” he wrote, “is simply one of distribution.”

In this way, these protests are revealing all sorts of new solidarities — not only between youth struggling to pay rent and seniors fearful of the cost of care, but between the disillusioned elite of European universities and the underpaid truck drivers of Italy, or the migrant teenager from the banlieues and the middle-class couples who can’t afford a child. All are part of the growing class of losers in the economy of today — an economy fatally consumed by presentism, unable and unwilling to consider the greater, long-term good.

Gerontocracy is certainly a contributor to that problem — after all, old people have less of a stake in the future. But in reality, the petty landlord milking tenants, the civil servant counting his days to retirement and the teenager looting Decathlon have much in common: They are all dogs fighting for scraps.

“Still working their way toward stable jobs, affording homes and having families, young people are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their job, it may well collapse the economy instead.”

This is perhaps the thing that earlier protesters in the historic youth uprisings in Nepal and India were able to see much more clearly than their counterparts in the more affluent regions of Europe, and may indeed be behind their relative success. Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic. There is little to separate a trucker who cannot pay for their gas from a student who cannot pay for their rent. Both are facing a profound existential crisis for which they bear little, if any, responsibility — a crisis their governments feel duty-bound to ignore.

It is in moments like this that the extraparliamentary politics of the street flourish. In some sense, this is a return to form for the politics of Europe. “We are quite used to the idea that everything should be oriented towards consensus,” Enrico Biale, an associate professor of political philosophy at University of Piemonte Orientale, told me. “Any form of strong protest is considered a challenge that needs to be contained aggressively.” But 50 years ago, discontented students flooded the ranks of the Red Army Faction and the Brigate Rosse , which terrorized fascist sympathizers (and plenty of bystanders) across the continent. In the ‘90s, Italy’s Pantera student movement paralyzed campuses and city centers over a bill to corporatize the universities; in the 1980s, French students did much the same . Those generations were closer to the violence of a real war, but they were arguably in no way as desperate as today’s youth.

That desperation had some of the analysts I spoke to on edge. There has been a different quality to these protests than past movements for change: a toxic mix of despair and nihilism. Many of those arrested for vandalism have no prior criminal record or connections to political movements. It’s unclear what, if anything, unites them, besides a complete lack of faith in conventional authorities and their processes. “We don’t trust the institutions of this government,” the October 17 Movement communique reads , and “we don’t trust the traditional political structures [which] have been trying to profit from and monopolize struggles for decades.”

This is the fruit of the short-termism natural to gerontocracy. And it is a boon to opportunists of all kinds — the criminal, the bigot, the fascist. Generational conflict is far more universal, and more inevitable, than a race war, and it has already become a recruiting tool for haters and nihilists of every description. Whether these protests, historic though they may be, result in any meaningful change is doubtful; Stockemer, for his part, is neither impressed nor optimistic. “There’s this big outbreak of rage,” he said. “Then we wait two years, and there’s another outbreak of rage.”

But with each chime of the futile clock, Europe’s youth becomes more disillusioned, and more radicalized. Eventually, that clock will run out — and then, no pension will be generous enough to spare the elderly their discomfort.
