stories.title: Smart glasses banned from Welsh Parliament after ruling they could be used for speeches
stories.summary: The decision comes while a review of the use of the devices in the Senedd takes place.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Jason O'Connell has used smart glasses to deliver speeches in the Senedd

Published 13 November 2026

The Senedd's presiding officer has in effect banned the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament, days after it emerged he would allow them to be used as a teleprompter.

Huw Irranca-Davies had ruled that using them in such a way was OK - provided he was alerted first - but Members of the Senedd (MS) have now been told he "will not be considering any other requests" to use the devices.

He said that will remain the case until a review into the use of the devices on the Senedd estate ends.

Reform's Jason O'Connell made headlines earlier this year after using the glasses to help him make a speech .

O'Connell, whose glasses do not include a camera, said he had voluntarily agreed not to use his device until the review is complete.

The MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr previously said he had started using glasses as a teleprompter to improve his speaking skills and to avoid looking down at his notes.

A letter from Irranca-Davies from 20 October, published in committee papers last week, said he had "determined that members may use smart glasses as a teleprompter in the chamber, provided that they give me advance notice".

Unlike other types of smart glasses that have caused controversy, like the ones above, O'Connell's do not have a camera built into them

On Tuesday, an official working for the presiding officer told MSs that "he will not be considering any other requests to use AI-equipped glasses in the Siambr until the review has reported".

They said: "Following further helpful discussions, no members will be using the technology until the review has been completed."

The official said the next stage of the Senedd Commission's review would include a consultation with MSs and staff, and would be completed by the end of 2026 with recommendations "brought forward in the new year".

O'Connell told BBC Wales after the decision: "I've voluntarily agreed to stop using the ones I'm using as a teleprompter until the review completes."

Asked how he felt about the matter, he said: "I'm ambivalent. They were a useful tool to be used on occasions.

"I was no way reliant on their use. But I look forward to using them again once the Senedd approves them."

The Senedd declined to elaborate on the statement to MSs after being asked why the presiding officer's stance had changed.

Reform is currently holding an unrelated boycott of Senedd proceedings , after its member Joe Martin was barred from speaking by Irranca-Davies, after Martin claimed in parliament that white people were being "replaced" in the UK.

The smart glasses decision was issued to MSs before the presiding officer's ruling on Martin was issued .

stories.title: Youth scheme branded 'failure' over success rate
stories.summary: Under half of those on the youth schemes took up work, education or training in London, new data suggests.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training (Neet), according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics

Published 13 November 2026

Less than half of young people supported by two government-backed youth schemes in London went on to take up further education, employment or training (Neet) opportunities, according to new data.

Only 1,100 of 2,600 young Londoners supported by the £20m Youth Guarantee Trailblazer scheme moved into further opportunities.

Former youth worker and Conservative peer Shaun Bailey said the scheme was a "failure" and called for more support for employers but Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was helping young people furthest from the labour market and that it was still "early days".

A major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out proposals for tackling the problem next week .

Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics.

London is one of eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazer areas in England already exploring ways to help young Neets.

More than £20m in government funding is being spent on a variety of initiatives across London, from youth hubs to mental health support.

The money is funding two trailblazer projects in London, one focused on care-experienced young people in 12 boroughs, and a broader scheme that works across the capital.

The Greater London Authority (GLA), which leads the projects, has shared the initial results from year one of the two schemes with the BBC.

By the end of June 2026, London's two trailblazer schemes had offered support to more than 2,600 young people.

The programme offers a range of support, including access to mental health and wellbeing services at colleges and universities, help moving into further education, work experience, careers events, mentoring and practical help finding a job.

The programme is funded for two years until the end of March 2027.

'Constant rejections'

Mattie Davies is a 19-year-old from London.

He recently left college, and since then, has struggled to find work.

"I applied to a good few thousand and it's constant rejections," Davies said.

He has found work as a delivery driver but he says the wage is not enough to pay his bills.

"Uber will take anyone and that's what I didn't want," he said. "I wanted a job I could go into and break down all of my barriers and build myself up as a person."

He has not been receiving support from London's two Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes.

Instead, he's been getting support from Millwall FC, where he plays football, and its youth programmes.

Mattie Davies says applying for jobs has been a struggle

Lord Bailey said the government should instead focus on helping businesses employ young people.

"Sixty per cent of young people not moving into full-time employment or education show you it's actually a failure," Lord Bailey said.

"That money would be better spent giving businesses some headroom so that they can actually afford to employ young people."

The skills minister said London's Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes were helping young people who face several challenges, such as mental health difficulties or experience of the care system.

"The fact that a lot of them are succeeding at the first opportunity is a good result," the minister said.

"It's worked exactly in the terms we set for it, which is young people who were furthest away from the labour market able to get back into the labour market, and learning about how we engage with some of those young people."

The eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazers in England have received a total of £90m in central government funding over the two years of the programme.

The trailblazers were part of the Labour government's plan to help 16 to 24-year-olds classed as Neet, whose number has been rising in recent years.

There were 125,949 Neets in London at the end of 2025, the highest number of any region in England, according to government data.

stories.title: Young, Welsh and into politics - but with different views on independence
stories.summary: A body has been set up to consider the case for Welsh independence as well as more devolved powers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Cerys and Patrick have different opinions on whether Wales should remain within the United Kingdom in the future

Published 12 November 2026

Cerys and Patrick have a lot in common. They're both young, Welsh, and very interested in politics.

The one thing they don't agree on is Wales' future within the United Kingdom.

A leading academic said the conversation around Welsh independence "has become normalised" amongst young people.

This week, the Plaid Cymru Welsh government set up a new body to consider the case for Welsh independence, as well as more devolution for Cardiff Bay.

For Patrick, he thinks his country is better off in the UK with more devolved powers, while Cerys believes an independent nation could offer more opportunities to people.

Nationalist party Plaid formed a government in Wales for the first after winning 46 seats during the May 2026 Senedd election .

While it hasn't called for a referendum on independence, the second line of its constitution says: "As the National Party of Wales, the party's aims shall be: to secure independence for Wales in Europe."

Pro-union party Reform UK is the second biggest in the Senedd after winning 34 seats in May's election.

Its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said voters "do not want to see Wales ripped out of the United Kingdom" and said the commission was "ridiculous".

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Young, Welsh and torn on independence

A recent poll by Survation for the pro-independence group YesCymru suggested people under 35 in Wales were more in favour of independence than their older peers.

"People feel left behind, especially my age," said Patrick, a 20-year-old student from Newport.

He added that he could understand why people were "energised and enthusiastic" about independence because of issues such as "student loans, the cost of living, the geopolitical scene".

But he said: "As of right now, I just do not think there is a case for it."

However, Patrick, said he would support further devolved powers for Wales within the union.

He said that "practical elements" such as whether there would be a border between Wales and England remain unanswered questions for him.

In Case You Misssed It - Young, political and torn on the future of the UK

12 November 2026

Are younger Welsh voters driving a shift towards independence? We examine why support is rising among under-35s, hear arguments from both sides and ask what the political future of Wales looks like.

For Cerys, learning to speak Welsh as an adult and broadening her understanding of history led to a "realisation" that Wales "in reality deserved a lot better than we had been given in the past and in the present".

"I think if we were independent, we could offer people more opportunity here," said the 35-year-old from Bridgend.

She added she'd like Wales to have further powers over policing and justice - a policy area currently controlled by Westminster.

"People seem to be kind of dangling the carrot of more devolution and never actually giving it to us," she said.

"More powers would be great but I will believe in those powers when I see them and until then, I think our best option is independence."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he was open to the idea of giving the Welsh government control of policing in Wales.

Cerys recently spoke at an independence rally in Aberystwyth alongside Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth

A leading academic from Cardiff University said "it's staggeringly important" that "young people are a majority in favour of independence".

"They see nothing strange or impossible about Wales becoming independent in the future," said Prof Laura McAllister, from the Welsh Governance Centre.

She said that there was "great scepticism" around the topic when you look at the opinions of people aged over 65, adding there was a "real demographic schism".

"There's going to need to be something much closer to support at least half the population supporting independence before there is any chance of a referendum being won," McAllister believes.

She added nobody "can afford to be complacent about the future of the union" because "the concept of the United Kingdom has no God-given right to survive in its current form".

"What we've seen in politics in recent times is that the potential for change is intrinsic to everything that happened," she said.

In 2024, McAllister co-chaired a commission which concluded Wales leaving the United Kingdom is a "viable" option .

Independence is one of the options being considered

With polling suggesting between 20% to 30% of people in Wales would be in favour of independence , external , academics have compared the current situation to Scotland in the years leading up to the independence referendum in 2014 .

"In some ways the situation here looks similar to Scotland in 2007," said Dr Jac Larner, a pollster and political analyst from Cardiff University, reflecting on when the Scottish National Party [SNP] took power.

"You might think now we have a party like Plaid Cymru, there's this inevitable march to this endless 50-50 that you see in Scotland, right?

"What's different here [in Wales] is that we still have a lot more hostility to the idea of devolution.

"You have about a third who want to get rid of the devolution altogether, maybe just less than a third who want independence."

Dr Jac Larner said attitudes towards independence and devolution are often driven by national identity

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "I have a vision for Wales, I support an independent Wales."

He said it was about "improving a lot of the people of Wales, tackling injustices, tackling unfairness, tackling inequalities, creating prosperity".

He added: "In the here and now, I deal with those issues dealing with the UK prime minister."

In October, the first ministers of Wales and Scotland met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Glasgow for the National Economic Council , where devolution and funding were discussed.

Ap Iorwerth said there was "a new understanding of the injustice of rail expenditure in Wales" from Burnham, as well as "a realisation that this hasn't been given enough attention politically by UK governments in the past".

Following the 2026 Autumn Budget , ap Iorwerth told BBC Wales there were " paltry sums of money coming on rail , when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".

A UK government spokesman said: "The prime minister passionately believes in our union and is optimistic about the future of the United Kingdom.

"Our position on referendums is clear - the prime minister is focused on practical solutions to help people with the cost of living and make a positive difference in people's everyday lives, not constitutional questions.

"Through the convening power of No10 North , the prime minister will build a constructive working relationship with each devolved government to explore how we can together contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

stories.title: Firm offers to fake artworks for wealthy migrants seeking UK 'talent' visas - BBC investigation
stories.summary: Going undercover to expose an elaborate fraud aimed at obtaining fast-track settlement for wealthy migrants.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: BBC undercover reporter is offered fake art and awards for 'talent' visa

Published 13 November 2026

Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.

The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.

Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.

We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.

No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.

In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.

A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.

"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.

Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.

The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.

A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".

They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

'It doesn't matter whether you're an artist'

The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.

Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.

Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media

During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:

At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying

The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application

For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims , when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.

The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.

A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."

An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".

Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".

The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.

About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.

The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.

Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".

We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent

Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.

"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.

Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.

Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.

During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.

Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.

The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.

It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.

Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.

This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.

Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.

The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.

The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.

The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal

During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.

The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.

"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."

He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".

When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.

"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".

"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."

The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".

Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.

Two visas revoked

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.

The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.

The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".

It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.

Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.

"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."

Part of the article, including artwork purporting to be by Silva Ndifon, that Molara Wood did not write

Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.

Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.

The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.

Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.

Cider maker Matilda Temperley said the budget had been "disappointing"

Published 13 November 2026

Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses.

Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset.

The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers.

Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs.

Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider.

More from Somerset

Christmas market fears as roadworks cause long delays Published 18 hours ago

Gritters out for the first time this autumn Published 1 day ago

No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says Published 1 day ago

"By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed.

She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it.

"We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020."

"The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said.

"That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards".

Isaac Stell says ultimately it will be the consumer who pays

Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole."

He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage.

"Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. "

Matthew Showering said like his apples - his business is growing

The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations.

"Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said.

"We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing."

While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention.

"We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible."

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider with his apple picker Johnny

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings.

Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs.

"We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county."

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks.

"But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief."

How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

Published 12 November 2026

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.

"The American people deserve answers," he added.

Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.

Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 12 hours ago

How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 1 day ago

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.

Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.

According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.

Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.

Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? Published 1 day ago

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 1 day ago

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.

It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.

Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.

Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.

Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.

The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.

Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.

Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.

Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.

Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.

Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US

Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer.

Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said.

Burberry said it made a pre-tax profit of £19m in the six months to 26 September after a loss of £48m a year before, as sales rose to £1.1bn. Sales rose 15% in China and 14% in the Americas but fell 1% in the Europe and Middle East region, partly due to the Iran war.

Schulman said Burberry’s focus on a “pyramid of pricing” ranging from more “affordable” scarves, starting from £195, and cotton-cashmere socks from £85, to its top-tier bags and coats, which can cost more than £9,000 for a leather version, had helped it achieve growth despite a tough market. Wealthy shoppers around the world are travelling less and being more cautious about spending, hitting luxury brand sales globally.

Sales of lightweight jackets and “tropical” gaberdine raincoats as well as its Cotswold range of leather bags and accessories featuring the brand’s famous check had proved popular.

Schulman said: “Luxury customers around the world are experiencing some fatigue with exorbitant pricing and in this context our strategy of having great value for money is resonating strongly with Chinese customers.”

“Burberry has always had a somewhat more democratic approach than some of our European peers and has a universal appeal,” he added.

Schulman said the brand had spent the last two years of its Burberry Forward strategy returning to its historical position at the “sweet spot in the luxury market”.

He said investment in locally relevant marketing, such as special product for China’s Valentine’s Day celebrations this spring and for the upcoming lunar new year, were also helping drive sales.

“It is no secret global tourism is down but the local customer has been spending in their respective regions,” Schulman said. “This is a trend we have been seeing all year long.”

While people were spending less as tourists which was hitting sales in discount outlets, Schulman said local spending was holding up in the brand’s flagship city centre stores including in London.

He said that while “nobody has a crystal ball” about whether customers would begin spending more freely, history suggested “this is a very cyclical business”.

stories.title: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
stories.summary: Politicians are worried about the outcomes of white, working-class pupils. But one school in Sunderland seems to have defied gravity
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds

Published 13 November 2026

Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.

Hetton's principal, Vicky Pinkney, says low incomes shouldn't mean poor results

The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English.

In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely.

What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results?

'Hard to move the dial'

From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift.

In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs.

Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome.

Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils.

Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says.

"It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim.

Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says.

Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education.

The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry , external found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success.

Morning quizzes and fish and chips evenings

So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control.

But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors.

So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.)

So, what is the school doing right?

After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy.

But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English.

It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney.

The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos.

For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard.

While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings.

There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject.

Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together.

It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff.

Pupils who feel they "belong" at school tend to perform better in their GCSEs, a government-commissioned study has found

And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs.

Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil.

Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves.

It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons".

High grades vs happiness?

But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success.

Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children.

The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education.

The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance.

Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.)

That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work.

The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades.

The likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing GCSEs has barely changed in many years, says John Jerrim, an education professor at University College London

But Macmillan, an education professor at University College London, also says that high grades shouldn't be seen as the only route into successful adult life. To suggest that sounds "demeaning" to some parents who didn't achieve high grades themselves, she thinks.

"Why have we created a structure where getting those maths and English GCSEs is so important to your life chances?" she says.

She wants the government to think about more entry-level apprenticeships and other on-the-job learning, so children with lower academic grades can still thrive.

Back in Sunderland, the 700 or so pupils at Hetton Academy have just arrived back in school after their half-term.

Does the principal think other places could replicate its success?

Absolutely, Pinkney says. And for her, it's personal: she points out that she too was raised by a single mother with little money, and still thrived academically.

"I feel really strongly about that. My school helped me to be able to achieve."

stories.title: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
stories.summary: The prime minister says the deal could be "more like the Brexit people thought they were voting for" in 2016.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 November 2026

Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.

The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".

The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others Published 2 days ago

UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC Published 6 days ago

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September

Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion? Published 1 day ago

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.

Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line.

"But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."

Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".

He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."

Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".

On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."

The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

stories.summary: Exclusive: Iran war has fuelled energy price rise and clouded outlook, driving up unemployment, says Clare Lombardelli Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned. Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.
